mainTopic: Which foods need a ברכה אחרונה, followed by teachings on eggs and on the health effects of foods
overview: The גמרא brings three views on which foods need a ברכה אחרונה: רב יצחק בר אבדימי excludes vegetables, רבי יצחק excludes only water, and רב פפא excludes nothing. A משנה says some things need a ברכה before but not after, and for רב פפא this refers to מצוות, or, for everyone, to fragrances. Since eggs were mentioned, the גמרא praises how nourishing eggs are, depending on how they are cooked. It explains that רבי עקיבא's nourishing boiled vegetable is a cabbage stalk. Then a ברייתא lists the health effects of foods, and the גמרא goes through it line by line: spleen and leeks, raw vegetables, small animals, the neck, cabbage and beets, and turnip. Along the way come רבי יצחק's two rules about vegetables before four hours, illustrated by a story with מר זוטרא, and a warning about small salted fish. Finally the גמרא returns to the משנה about drinking water לצמאו. רב אידי בר אבין's answer continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Eggs and meat: שהכל before, בורא נפשות after, but no blessing after vegetables
steps.stepSummary: רב יצחק בר אבדימי, quoting רב, rules that eggs and meat need שהכל before and בורא נפשות after, while vegetables need no blessing after.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יצחק בר אבדימי said in the name of our teacher (רב): Over an egg and over kinds of meat, one first says 'שהכל,' and afterwards 'בורא נפשות רבות.' But vegetables do not get a blessing after.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ruling from רב about blessings on eggs and meat. It also says vegetables get no ברכה אחרונה at all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Eggs and meat do not grow from the ground, so before eating them you say שהכל. After eating them you say the short after-blessing, בורא נפשות. Vegetables, however, are treated as too minor to need any blessing after eating.

keyTerms.meaning: The blessing 'by Whose word all things came to be'
The short after-blessing 'Who creates many forms of life'

steps.confusionAlert: 'יַרְקָא לָא' does not mean vegetables get no blessing at all. They still get a blessing before eating. This view only says they get no blessing AFTER eating.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב יִצְחָק בַּר אַבְדִּימִי מִשּׁוּם רַבֵּינוּ:
phrases.english: Rav Yitzchak bar Avdimi said in the name of our teacher:
phrases.notes: 'Our teacher' (רבינו) here refers to רב.

phrases.english: Over the egg and over kinds of meat,
at the beginning one says 'Shehakol',
and at the end, 'Who creates many forms of life, etc.'
But vegetables, no (no blessing after).

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יִצְחָק בַּר אַבְדִּימִי מִשּׁוּם רַבֵּינוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens the discussion of after-blessings for eggs, meat and vegetables.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Eggs and meat get שהכל before and בורא נפשות after. Vegetables get no ברכה אחרונה.

steps.title: רבי יצחק: even vegetables need a blessing after, but not water
steps.stepSummary: רבי יצחק disagrees and says vegetables also need בורא נפשות after eating, but water does not.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי יצחק said: Even vegetables get a blessing after. But water does not.
steps.whatsHappening: A second אמורא argues and widens the rule to include vegetables. He still leaves water out.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יצחק moves the line one step further than the first view. Vegetables are significant enough for a blessing after eating. Water, though, is still too minor for one.

phrases.english: And Rabbi Yitzchak said: Even vegetables (get a blessing after),
but water, no.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Disagrees with step 1 and adds vegetables to the list.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Vegetables need a ברכה אחרונה. Water does not.

steps.title: רב פפא: even water needs a blessing after
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא goes furthest and says even water needs a ברכה אחרונה.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רב פפא said: Even water gets a blessing after.
steps.whatsHappening: A third אמורא widens the rule all the way to include water.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now there are three levels. The first view excludes vegetables and water, רבי יצחק excludes only water, and רב פפא excludes nothing. This matters later, because רב פפא seems to leave no food without an after-blessing.

phrases.english: And Rav Pappa said: Even water (gets a blessing after).

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes even further than step 2 and adds water.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Even water needs a ברכה אחרונה.
steps.whyThisMatters: Because this view is so broad, it becomes the target of the challenge in step 6.

steps.title: How two sages acted, with a memory aid
steps.stepSummary: מר זוטרא followed רב יצחק בר אבדימי, and רב שימי בר אשי followed רבי יצחק. A memory aid helps keep them straight.
steps.simpleTranslation: מר זוטרא acted like רב יצחק בר אבדימי, and רב שימי בר אשי acted like רבי יצחק. Your memory aid: one like two, and two like one.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא reports what two אמוראים actually did in practice. It then gives a trick for remembering who followed whom.
steps.deeperAnalysis: מר זוטרא did not say a blessing after vegetables, and רב שימי בר אשי did. The memory aid counts names. מר זוטרא has one name and followed a sage with two names (יצחק בר אבדימי). רב שימי בר אשי has two names and followed a sage with one name (רבי יצחק).
steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up רב יצחק בר אבדימי (the first view) with רבי יצחק (the second view). They are different people with different opinions. That is exactly why the memory aid is needed.

phrases.aramaic: מָר זוּטְרָא עָבֵיד כְּרַב יִצְחָק בַּר אַבְדִּימִי,
phrases.english: Mar Zutra acted like Rav Yitzchak bar Avdimi,

phrases.aramaic: וְרַב שִׁימִי בַּר אָשֵׁי עָבֵיד כְּרַבִּי יִצְחָק.
phrases.english: and Rav Shimi bar Ashi acted like Rabbi Yitzchak.
And your memory aid: one like two, and two like one.
phrases.notes: Mar Zutra (one name) followed a two-name sage. Rav Shimi bar Ashi (two names) followed a one-name sage.

steps.triggerLanguage: מָר זוּטְרָא עָבֵיד כְּרַב יִצְחָק בַּר אַבְדִּימִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows how steps 1 and 2 were followed in practice.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In practice there were sages who followed each of the first two views.

steps.title: רב אשי tries to satisfy all opinions
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי says that when he remembers, he acts like all the views and says a blessing after everything, even water.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said: As for me, when I remember, I act like all of them.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי tells us his personal practice: when he remembers, he says a blessing after eating or drinking anything.
steps.deeperAnalysis: By following the broadest view (רב פפא), רב אשי covers every opinion. Saying a blessing after water fits רב פפא, and it also covers vegetables. His words 'when I remember' suggest this was an extra effort, not a firm rule he always kept.

keyTerms.meaning: At a time when I remember

steps.whatToRemember: There are three views on ברכה אחרונה: (1) רב יצחק בר אבדימי: not after vegetables. (2) רבי יצחק: after vegetables, but not water. (3) רב פפא: even after water. רב אשי tried to satisfy all of them.

phrases.english: Rav Ashi said: As for me,
at a time when I remember, I act like all of them.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב אָשֵׁי: אֲנָא, זִמְנָא דְּכִי מִדְּכַרְנָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a practical approach that satisfies all three views from steps 1 to 3.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When possible, say a blessing after everything, so that you satisfy every opinion.

steps.title: A source says some foods need no blessing after, which is a problem for רב פפא
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes a source saying some foods need a blessing before but not after. That fits the first two views, but under רב פפא nothing seems to be left out.
steps.simpleTranslation: We learned: Anything that needs a blessing after needs a blessing before, and there are things that need a blessing before but not after. That works for רב יצחק בר אבדימי, since it leaves out vegetables. It works for רבי יצחק, since it leaves out water. But according to רב פפא, what does it leave out?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב פפא from an earlier teaching. It says some foods need a blessing before but not after, and asks what such a food could be if even water needs a blessing after.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The source assumes there is a group of foods with no ברכה אחרונה. For the first view that group is vegetables, and for רבי יצחק it is water. רב פפא gives every food and drink a blessing after, so the source's words seem to have nothing to describe.

keyTerms.meaning: It works out well for (introduces what fits before the problem)

steps.confusionAlert: The question is not 'why does רב פפא disagree?' It is narrower: the source says some foods are left out, so under רב פפא, which ones are they?

phrases.english: We learned: Anything that needs a blessing after it
needs a blessing before it,
and there are things that need a blessing before them
but do not need a blessing after them.

phrases.aramaic: בִּשְׁלָמָא לְרַב יִצְחָק בַּר אַבְדִּימִי, לְאַפּוֹקֵי יַרְקָא.
phrases.english: It works out for Rav Yitzchak bar Avdimi: it comes to exclude vegetables.
For Rabbi Yitzchak: it comes to exclude water.
But according to Rav Pappa, what does it exclude?
phrases.notes: This is the challenge. The next step answers it.

steps.triggerLanguage: בִּשְׁלָמָא לְרַב יִצְחָק בַּר אַבְדִּימִי, לְאַפּוֹקֵי יַרְקָא. לְרַבִּי יִצְחָק, לְאַפּוֹקֵי מַיָּא, אֶלָּא לְרַב פָּפָּא, לְאַפּוֹקֵי מַאי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses an earlier source to test the three views, and finds a problem only for רב פפא (step 3).
steps.kashyaTarget: רב פפא's view that even water needs a ברכה אחרונה (step 3)
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The source says some foods need a blessing before but not after. If even water gets a blessing after, no food fits that description, so the source's words would describe nothing.
steps.whyThisMatters: This challenge shows that the earlier source assumes some foods have no blessing after. Any view has to explain which foods those are.

steps.title: The rule refers to מצוות
steps.stepSummary: Under רב פפא, the phrase 'some things need a blessing before but not after' refers to מצוות.
steps.simpleTranslation: It comes to exclude מצוות.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question from step 6. Even if every food needs a ברכה אחרונה, the rule still has a purpose: it teaches about מצוות.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Before doing a מצוה we say a ברכה, such as 'אשר קדשנו במצותיו'. Afterward we usually say nothing. So according to רב פפא, the words 'there are things with a blessing before but not after' were never about food. They were about מצוות.

keyTerms.meaning: to exclude; this is what the rule comes to leave out
commandments, which get a ברכה before they are done but not after

phrases.english: To exclude מצוות.
phrases.notes: A ברכה is said before doing a מצוה, but none is said after it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 6 by moving the rule's 'exception' from food to מצוות.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reassigning the scope of the source
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Under רב פפא, the phrase 'some need a blessing before and not after' seems to have nothing left to describe.
steps.terutzMaskana: It refers to מצוות, which get a ברכה only before.

steps.title: But in ארץ ישראל they bless after removing תפילין
steps.stepSummary: The people of ארץ ישראל say a ברכה after taking off תפילין, so for them at least one מצוה has a blessing afterward. What does the rule exclude for them?
steps.simpleTranslation: And for the people of the West (ארץ ישראל), who after removing their תפילין recite 'Who sanctified us with His commandments and commanded us to keep His statutes,' what does it come to exclude?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the answer it just gave. For בני מערבא, תפילין get an after-blessing, so 'מצוות' as a whole is no longer a clean example of a blessing before and none after.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 7's answer treats מצוות as the category with a ברכה before and none after. The custom in ארץ ישראל of blessing 'לשמור חקיו' after removing תפילין gives one מצוה an after-blessing, so for them that answer no longer covers מצוות as a whole. Tosafot notes that even בני מערבא blessed afterward only on תפילין, because the Torah calls them a חקה, and not on ציצית, לולב or סוכה; Tosafot asks why the גמרא did not simply answer 'the other מצוות'. The גמרא instead gives an answer that works for everyone (step 9).

keyTerms.meaning: 'people of the West' — the scholars of ארץ ישראל
to keep His statutes — the ending of their after-blessing

phrases.english: And for the people of the West (Eretz Yisrael),
who, after they remove their tefillin,
recite: 'Who sanctified us with His commandments
and commanded us to keep His statutes,'
what does it come to exclude?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges step 7's answer by pointing to a custom that gives תפילין an after-blessing.
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer that the rule excludes מצוות
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: For בני מערבא, תפילין have a ברכה afterward, so מצוות as a whole cannot be the excluded category.

steps.title: The rule refers to fragrances
steps.stepSummary: For everyone, the rule excludes fragrances, which get a ברכה before smelling but never after.
steps.simpleTranslation: To exclude fragrances.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a new answer that works for everyone: the rule is talking about pleasant smells.
steps.deeperAnalysis: We say a ברכה before smelling something fragrant. No one, not even בני מערבא or רב פפא, requires a ברכה after smelling. So fragrances are a category with a blessing before and none after, and the rule has a real meaning for all views.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is the practical rule today: we say a ברכה before smelling בשמים, but nothing afterward.

phrases.english: To exclude fragrances.
phrases.notes: A ברכה is said before smelling, never after.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 8 with a category that has no after-blessing under any custom.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Since even מצוות have an after-blessing for בני מערבא, the rule seems to exclude nothing.
steps.terutzMaskana: Fragrances never get an after-blessing, so the rule refers to them.

steps.title: An egg is better than an equal amount of other food
steps.stepSummary: רבי ינאי quotes רבי: an egg is more nourishing than any other food of the same size.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי ינאי said in the name of רבי: Anything that is the size of an egg — an egg is better than it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא changes topic. Eggs were just mentioned in רב יצחק בר אבדימי's ruling (step 1), so it now brings sayings about how valuable eggs are, starting with רבי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is not a halachic ruling about ברכות. It is a statement about health. Take any food measuring a כביצה: a real egg of that size is more nourishing.

keyTerms.meaning: the volume of an egg, a common measurement

phrases.english: Rabbi Yannai said in the name of Rabbi (Yehuda HaNasi):
Anything that is the size of an egg —
an egg is better than it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new topic, connected only by the mention of eggs in רב יצחק בר אבדימי's ruling in step 1.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An egg is more nourishing than an equal volume of any other food.

steps.title: רבין: a soft-cooked egg beats six measures of flour
steps.stepSummary: רבין, arriving from ארץ ישראל, says a lightly cooked egg is better than six measures of fine flour.
steps.simpleTranslation: When רבין came, he said: A lightly cooked egg is better than six לוג of fine flour.
steps.whatsHappening: Another teaching about eggs, this one brought by רבין from ארץ ישראל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבין praises eggs even more strongly. A lightly cooked egg is worth more than a large amount of fine flour, about six לוג.

keyTerms.meaning: 'when he came' — used for a scholar arriving from ארץ ישראל to בבל

phrases.english: When Ravin came (from Eretz Yisrael), he said:
A lightly cooked egg is better
than six log of fine flour.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a further statement praising eggs.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A lightly cooked egg is better than six log of fine flour.

steps.title: רב דימי: the value depends on how the egg is cooked
steps.stepSummary: רב דימי ranks eggs by cooking method: soft-cooked beats six measures, roasted beats four, and boiled beats any equal amount except meat.
steps.simpleTranslation: When רב דימי came, he said: A lightly cooked egg is better than six; a roasted one, than four; a cooked one — anything the size of an egg, an egg is better than it, except for meat.
steps.whatsHappening: רב דימי combines the earlier sayings and sorts them by how the egg is prepared.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There are three levels. A soft-cooked egg is the best, worth six measures. A roasted egg is worth four. A fully boiled egg is only better than an equal amount of other food. This boiled-egg case is רבי's statement from step 10, with one limit added: meat is even better.
steps.whatToRemember: The ברכה rule 'some things need a ברכה before but not after' refers to מצוות, or, for everyone, to fragrances. After that, the גמרא praises eggs: the softer the egg, the more nourishing, and only meat beats a boiled egg.
steps.confusionAlert: The numbers 'six' and 'four' refer to measures (לוג) of fine flour, not six or four eggs.

phrases.english: When Rav Dimi came (from Eretz Yisrael), he said:
A lightly cooked egg is better than six (log of flour);
a roasted egg — than four;
a cooked egg — anything that is the size of an egg,
an egg is better than it,
except for meat.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Combines and refines the sayings of רבי and רבין by sorting them by cooking method, and adds an exception for meat.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An egg's value depends on how it is cooked: soft beats six measures of flour, roasted beats four, and boiled beats any equal amount of food except meat.

steps.title: Back to the משנה: רבי עקיבא on boiled vegetables
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the opening words of רבי עקיבא's statement in the משנה so it can discuss it.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי עקיבא says: even if he ate boiled vegetables, etc.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to quote a line from the משנה. This is a setup line that gets ready for the question in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the משנה, רבי עקיבא rules that even boiled vegetables (שלק) get the full three ברכות of ברכת המזון if they are a person's main food. The גמרא quotes only the first words, ending with כו׳ ("etc."), to point to the full statement.

keyTerms.meaning: "Etc.": the rest of the quote is left out

phrases.english: Rabbi Akiva says
Even if he ate boiled vegetables, etc.
phrases.notes: The full line in the משנה: if it is his main food, he says the three ברכות.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא אוֹמֵר אֲפִילּוּ אָכַל שֶׁלֶק
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the egg statements back to a new line in the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Boiled vegetables that are someone's main food get the full ברכת המזון, according to רבי עקיבא.

steps.title: Can a boiled vegetable really be a main food?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whether any boiled vegetable is filling enough to count as real food.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is there really anything that, when boiled, counts as real sustaining food?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רבי עקיבא's case. Is there any boiled vegetable that actually nourishes like a meal?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Boiled vegetables seem too light to be a real meal. If none can be a main food, רבי עקיבא's ruling would describe a case that never happens. So the גמרא needs a real example.

phrases.english: And is there anything
that, when boiled, is real sustenance?

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמִי אִיכָּא מִידֵּי דְּהָוֵה שֶׁלֶק מְזוֹנֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions whether the case in the quoted משנה is realistic.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי עקיבא's case of a boiled vegetable that is someone's main food
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Boiled vegetables do not seem to nourish anyone, so the case looks impossible.

steps.title: רב אשי: it means a cabbage stalk
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי explains that the משנה is talking about a cabbage stalk, which really is nourishing.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said: they taught this about a cabbage stalk.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי answers the question by naming the vegetable the משנה means: a cabbage stalk.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A cabbage stalk, even boiled, is filling enough to work as a main food. So רבי עקיבא's case is real, and his ruling stands.

keyTerms.meaning: "They taught": tells us what case the source is about

phrases.english: Rav Ashi said:
They taught it about a cabbage stalk.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב אָשֵׁי בְּקֶלַח שֶׁל כְּרוּב שָׁנוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 14.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the case: the משנה is about one specific vegetable
steps.terutzHavaAmina: No boiled vegetable can be real food, so רבי עקיבא's case never happens.
steps.terutzMaskana: A boiled cabbage stalk is nourishing, so the case is real.
steps.whatToRemember: רבי עקיבא's 'boiled vegetable that is a main food' means a cabbage stalk, according to רב אשי.

steps.title: A ברייתא on foods that help and harm the body
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא lists the health effects of different foods: spleen, leeks, raw vegetables, small foods, whole creatures, cabbage, beets and turnip.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן taught: spleen is good for the teeth and bad for the intestines. Leeks are bad for the teeth and good for the intestines. All raw vegetables make a person pale. Anything small stunts growth. Any whole living creature restores the soul, and anything close to the soul restores the soul. Cabbage is for food and beets are for healing. Woe to the house that turnip passes through.
steps.whatsHappening: Since cabbage was just called nourishing, the גמרא brings a ברייתא of health facts about foods, including cabbage.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא first pairs two foods with opposite effects: spleen helps teeth but hurts the intestines, and leeks do the reverse. Then it gives general rules: raw vegetables make you pale, foods that are not fully grown stunt growth, and a creature eaten whole (רש״י: a small whole fish) or meat near the 'soul' (רש״י: near the throat) is strengthening. It ends by praising cabbage and beets and warning against turnip.

keyTerms.meaning: Makes a person pale or sickly

steps.confusionAlert: Here נפש does not mean 'soul' in the spiritual sense. 'כל נפש' is a creature eaten whole, and 'קרוב לנפש' is meat from near the throat, according to רש״י. Both are health claims, not spiritual ones.

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
Spleen is good for the teeth
and bad for the intestines.
Leeks are bad for the teeth
and good for the intestines.
All raw vegetables make one pale,
and anything small (not fully grown) stunts growth,
and any whole living creature restores the soul,
phrases.notes: רש״י explains: for example, a small fish eaten whole.

phrases.aramaic: וְכׇל קָרוֹב לַנֶּפֶשׁ מֵשִׁיב אֶת הַנֶּפֶשׁ.
phrases.english: and anything close to the soul restores the soul.
phrases.notes: רש״י explains: meat from near the throat.

phrases.english: Cabbage is for nourishment,
and beets are for healing.
Woe to the house
that turnip passes through.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Connected by topic: cabbage, just called nourishing, appears in this ברייתא as 'for food.'
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Foods have specific health effects: spleen and leeks have opposite effects, raw vegetables cause paleness, small foods stunt growth, whole creatures strengthen, cabbage nourishes, beets heal, and turnip is harmful.

steps.title: How can one eat spleen without harm?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the spleen line from the ברייתא and asks how to get its benefit while avoiding its harm.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Master said: spleen is good for the teeth and bad for the intestines. What is the remedy for it?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא re-quotes the spleen line to ask a practical question: how do you get the good part without the bad part?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא said spleen helps the teeth but hurts the intestines. The גמרא wants a way to keep the benefit and avoid the damage.

phrases.english: The Master said:
Spleen is good for the teeth
and bad for the intestines.
What is its remedy?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Picks up the first line of the ברייתא to work out a practical fix.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A way to get the dental benefit of spleen without harming the intestines.

steps.title: Chew the spleen and spit it out
steps.stepSummary: Chew the spleen for the teeth, then spit it out instead of swallowing it.
steps.simpleTranslation: He should chew it and throw it away.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers: chew the spleen, then spit it out.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Chewing gives the teeth the benefit. Because the spleen is never swallowed, it never reaches the intestines and cannot harm them.

keyTerms.meaning: He should throw it away (spit it out)

phrases.english: He should chew it and throw it away.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question about spleen.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Chew it for the teeth, then spit it out so it never reaches the intestines.

steps.title: How can one eat leeks without harm?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the leek line and asks the same question: how do you avoid the harm?
steps.simpleTranslation: Leeks are bad for the teeth and good for the intestines. What is the remedy for them?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא does the same thing for leeks, which are the opposite case: bad for the teeth, good for the intestines.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With leeks the problem is reversed. The teeth are what need protecting, while the intestines should still get the benefit.

phrases.english: Leeks are bad for the teeth
and good for the intestines.
What is its remedy?

steps.triggerLanguage: כְּרֵישִׁין קָשִׁין לַשִּׁינַּיִם וְיָפִין לִבְנֵי מֵעַיִם מַאי תַּקַּנְתֵּיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Same pattern as step 17, now for the opposite food.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A way to get the benefit of leeks for the intestines without harming the teeth.

steps.title: Boil the leeks and swallow them
steps.stepSummary: Boil the leeks and swallow them without chewing, so the teeth are not harmed.
steps.simpleTranslation: He should boil them and swallow them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers: boil the leeks soft and swallow them whole.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Swallowing without chewing keeps the leeks away from the teeth, while the intestines still get the benefit. This is the mirror image of the spleen fix.
steps.whatToRemember: The two fixes mirror each other. Spleen: chew it and spit it out, so only the teeth get it. Leeks: boil them and swallow them, so only the intestines get them.

phrases.english: He should boil them and swallow them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question about leeks.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Boil them soft and swallow them without chewing, so they skip the teeth but still reach the intestines.

steps.title: Raw vegetables cause paleness only after bloodletting
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the ברייתא's line that raw vegetables make one pale. רבי יצחק limits it to the first meal after הקזה.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'All raw vegetables make a person pale.' רבי יצחק said: this refers to the first meal after bloodletting.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא picks up the next line of the ברייתא about raw vegetables. רבי יצחק explains when this warning applies.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Read alone, the ברייתא sounds like raw vegetables are always harmful. רבי יצחק narrows it to one weak moment: the first meal after הקזה, when the body needs strengthening food.
steps.confusionAlert: רבי יצחק is not saying raw vegetables are always unhealthy. His point is that the paleness warning applies only to the first meal after הקזה.

phrases.english: All raw vegetables make one pale,
phrases.notes: Quoted from the ברייתא in step 16

phrases.english: Rabbi Yitzchak said:
At the first meal after bloodletting.

steps.triggerLanguage: כׇּל יָרָק חַי מוֹרִיק, אָמַר רַבִּי יִצְחָק
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues going through the lines of the ברייתא from step 16, now reaching raw vegetables.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The ברייתא's warning that raw vegetables cause paleness applies to the first meal after bloodletting.

steps.title: Do not talk with someone who ate vegetables early in the day
steps.stepSummary: רבי יצחק rules that it is forbidden to talk with a person who ate vegetables before the fourth hour of the day.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי יצחק said: anyone who eats vegetables before four hours of the day, it is forbidden to talk with him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second teaching of רבי יצחק about vegetables. It sets up a question about the reason, which comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is a new rule about social conduct, not health. The time limit is the first four hours of the day. No reason is given yet, so the גמרא will ask for one.

keyTerms.meaning: Before the end of the fourth hour of the day

phrases.english: And Rabbi Yitzchak said:
Anyone who eats vegetables
before four hours of the day,
it is forbidden to talk with him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Another teaching of the same speaker, רבי יצחק, about vegetables.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: It is forbidden to converse with someone who ate vegetables before the fourth hour of the day.

steps.title: Why is it forbidden to talk with him?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the reason behind רבי יצחק's rule.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why talking with such a person would be forbidden. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Eating vegetables is not a sin, so a ban on talking with the eater needs explaining. The answer will matter later, in the story with מר זוטרא.

phrases.english: What is the reason?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the reason behind step 22.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The reason it is forbidden to speak with one who ate vegetables early in the day.

steps.title: Because of the smell
steps.stepSummary: The reason is the vegetable smell on his breath.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because of the smell.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the problem is the bad smell from his mouth.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Early in the day, other people have not eaten yet, so the vegetable smell on his breath bothers them. The rule is about not bothering others. It is not a ban on the food itself.
steps.whyThisMatters: Because this reason is about bothering others, the story below can challenge מר זוטרא's behavior based on it.

phrases.english: Because of the smell.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 23.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The ban exists because of the unpleasant smell from his mouth.

steps.title: Eating raw vegetables early in the day is forbidden
steps.stepSummary: A third teaching of רבי יצחק: a person may not eat raw vegetables before four hours of the day.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי יצחק said: it is forbidden for a person to eat raw vegetables before four hours of the day.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings another teaching of רבי יצחק. This one bans the eating itself.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule in step 22 was about talking with the eater, and it covered any vegetables. This rule is about the eating itself, and it covers raw vegetables. These are two separate rules, and the story will depend on that difference.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not merge this with step 22. Step 22 forbids talking with the eater because of the smell. This step forbids eating raw vegetables at all.

phrases.english: And Rabbi Yitzchak said:
It is forbidden for a person to eat raw vegetables
before four hours of the day.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רַבִּי יִצְחָק: אָסוּר לְאָדָם שֶׁיֹּאכַל יָרָק חַי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A separate teaching of רבי יצחק, different from step 22.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Eating raw vegetables before the fourth hour of the day is forbidden.

steps.title: Three sages are served raw vegetables early in the day
steps.stepSummary: אמימר and רב אשי eat the raw vegetables served early in the day. מר זוטרא does not.
steps.simpleTranslation: אמימר, מר זוטרא and רב אשי were sitting. Raw vegetables were brought before them before four hours of the day. אמימר and רב אשי ate, and מר זוטרא did not eat.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a story that sets up a question. Two sages eat raw vegetables early in the day, and one refuses.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The facts match רבי יצחק's rules exactly: raw vegetables, before four hours. מר זוטרא's refusal invites a question about which rule he is following.

phrases.aramaic: אַמֵּימָר וּמָר זוּטְרָא וְרַב אָשֵׁי הֲווֹ יָתְבִי,
phrases.english: Ameimar, Mar Zutra and Rav Ashi were sitting,
they brought before them raw vegetables
before four hours of the day.
Ameimar and Rav Ashi ate,
and Mar Zutra did not eat.

steps.triggerLanguage: אַמֵּימָר וּמָר זוּטְרָא וְרַב אָשֵׁי הֲווֹ יָתְבִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A real-life case that applies רבי יצחק's teachings.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Story setup: מר זוטרא refused raw vegetables before four hours while his colleagues ate.

steps.title: His colleagues challenge his reason for not eating
steps.stepSummary: His colleagues guess that מר זוטרא is following the smell rule. They point out that he is talking with them even though they ate.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said to him: what is your thinking? Is it because רבי יצחק said that anyone who eats vegetables before four hours, it is forbidden to talk with him because of the smell? But we are eating, and you are talking with us!
steps.whatsHappening: אמימר and רב אשי challenge מר זוטרא. If the smell rule is his reason, his own behavior contradicts it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: They assume he avoided eating so that people could still talk to him. But the smell rule really targets the listener: he should not talk with those who ate. Yet he is chatting with them right now, so that cannot be his reason.

phrases.english: They said to him: What is your thinking?
That Rabbi Yitzchak said

phrases.aramaic: כׇּל הָאוֹכֵל יָרָק קוֹדֶם אַרְבַּע שָׁעוֹת
phrases.english: anyone who eats vegetables before four hours
it is forbidden to talk with him because of the smell?
But look, we are eating,
and you are talking with us!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions מר זוטרא's refusal from step 26, using the rule from steps 22 and 24.
steps.kashyaTarget: מר זוטרא's refusal to eat, assuming it rests on the smell rule
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If he cared about the smell rule, he would not be talking with people who just ate vegetables. His behavior is inconsistent.

steps.title: מר זוטרא follows the other rule of רבי יצחק
steps.stepSummary: מר זוטרא explains that he follows רבי יצחק's other rule, which bans eating raw vegetables early in the day.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to them: I hold like the other teaching of רבי יצחק. For רבי יצחק said: it is forbidden for a person to eat raw vegetables before four hours of the day.
steps.whatsHappening: מר זוטרא answers that his reason was never the smell. He follows the separate ban on eating raw vegetables before four hours.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The challenge only worked against the smell rule, which governs talking. The rule in step 25 governs eating, so it explains his refusal. It does not require him to stop talking with those who did eat.

keyTerms.meaning: I hold, this is my view

steps.whatToRemember: רבי יצחק has two separate rules. One: do not talk with someone who ate vegetables before four hours, because of the smell. Two: do not eat raw vegetables before four hours. מר זוטרא followed the second rule, so he did not eat but still spoke with his colleagues.

phrases.english: He said to them:

phrases.aramaic: אֲנָא כְּאִידַּךְ דְּרַבִּי יִצְחָק סְבִירָא לִי.
phrases.english: I hold like the other teaching of Rabbi Yitzchak.
For Rabbi Yitzchak said:
It is forbidden for a person to eat raw vegetables
before four hours of the day.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲנָא כְּאִידַּךְ דְּרַבִּי יִצְחָק סְבִירָא לִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 27 by pointing to the rule in step 25.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Switching the source: his behavior rests on a different teaching of the same אמורא
steps.terutzHavaAmina: His colleagues assumed he was following the smell rule about talking.
steps.terutzMaskana: He follows the ban on eating raw vegetables before four hours, which fits his talking with them.

steps.title: Small animals stunt growth, even a goat worth a זוז
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes 'anything small stunts growth,' and רב חסדא says this includes even a young goat worth a זוז.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'Anything small makes one small.' רב חסדא said: even a young goat worth a זוז.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes a new line from the list of food sayings. רב חסדא tells us how far that line reaches.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The line says that eating young, small animals is bad for a person's growth. A goat worth a whole זוז sounds valuable, so you might think it is big enough. רב חסדא says it still counts as 'small.'

keyTerms.meaning: Something small makes a person small (stunts growth)

phrases.english: Anything small makes one small,
phrases.notes: Quoted from the list of food sayings.

phrases.english: Rav Chisda said:
Even a young goat worth a zuz.
phrases.notes: Even though it costs a full זוז, it is still a 'small' animal.

steps.triggerLanguage: כׇּל קָטָן מַקְטִין, אָמַר רַב חִסְדָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on from רבי יצחק's teachings to explain another line from the food list.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The rule 'anything small stunts growth' includes even a young goat worth a זוז.

steps.title: The rule applies only before the animal reaches a quarter of its size
steps.stepSummary: The rule only applies to an animal that has not yet reached a quarter of its full size. After that there is no concern.
steps.simpleTranslation: We only said this when it has not reached a quarter of its size. But if it has reached a quarter, we have no problem with it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא puts a limit on רב חסדא's rule. It tells us when an animal stops counting as 'small.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 29 made the rule wide, so even a fairly costly goat counts. This step sets the cutoff. Once the animal has grown to one quarter of its adult size, eating it is fine.

keyTerms.meaning: We only said this when (a limiting phrase)
A quarter (of the animal's full size)
We have no problem with it

phrases.aramaic: וְלָא אֲמַרַן אֶלָּא דְּלֵית בֵּיהּ רִבְעָא,
phrases.english: And we only said this when it does not have a quarter,
phrases.notes: A quarter of its adult size.

phrases.english: but if it has a quarter —
we have no problem with it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Limits רב חסדא's rule from step 29.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An animal that has reached a quarter of its full size no longer counts as 'small.'

steps.title: Any whole creature restores the soul, even tiny reed fish
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes 'any creature restores the soul,' and רב פפא says this includes even tiny fish from the reeds.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'Any creature restores the soul.' רב פפא said: even the little fish from among the reeds.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the next line of the list. רב פפא shows how wide it goes.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This line speaks about a creature eaten whole. You might think a very tiny fish gives no benefit. רב פפא says that even these tiny fish are healthy, because they are fully grown at their small size.

keyTerms.meaning: Restores the soul, refreshes and strengthens a person

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix this up with step 29. 'Small' there means a young animal that is not fully grown. These tiny fish are adults that simply stay small.

phrases.english: Any creature restores the soul,
phrases.notes: Meaning a creature eaten whole.

phrases.english: Rav Pappa said:
Even little fish from among the reeds.

steps.triggerLanguage: כׇּל נֶפֶשׁ מֵשִׁיב נֶפֶשׁ, אָמַר רַב פָּפָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves to the next line in the same list.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Even tiny reed fish count as a creature that restores the soul.

steps.title: The part close to the soul is the neck
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes 'whatever is close to the soul restores the soul,' and רב אחא בר יעקב says this means the neck.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'Whatever is close to the soul restores the soul.' רב אחא בר יעקב said: the neck.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes another line and asks which part of the animal it means. רב אחא בר יעקב answers that it is the neck.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'Close to the soul' is a vague phrase. רב אחא בר יעקב makes it concrete: the neck, which sits near the animal's vital organs. So meat from the neck is the healthiest.

keyTerms.meaning: What is close to the soul (near the vital organs)

phrases.aramaic: כׇּל הַקָּרוֹב לַנֶּפֶשׁ מֵשִׁיב אֶת הַנֶּפֶשׁ,
phrases.english: Whatever is close to the soul restores the soul,
Rav Acha bar Yaakov said:
The neck.

steps.triggerLanguage: כׇּל הַקָּרוֹב לַנֶּפֶשׁ מֵשִׁיב אֶת הַנֶּפֶשׁ, אָמַר רַב אַחָא בַּר יַעֲקֹב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves to the next line in the same list.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The part 'close to the soul' is the neck.

steps.title: רבא asks his servant for meat from the neck
steps.stepSummary: רבא told his servant to make an effort to bring him meat from near the place of the blessing, meaning the neck where the animal was slaughtered.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said to his attendant: When you bring me a piece of meat, make an effort to bring it from the area close to the place of the 'ברוך.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows רבא putting step 32 into practice. He asks for neck meat.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'The place of ברוך' is the neck. That is where the שחיטה is done, and the שוחט says a ברכה there. רבא's request backs up the idea that neck meat is the best for a person's health.

keyTerms.meaning: Make an effort, take the trouble
The place of the ברכה, the neck where the שחיטה is done

steps.whatToRemember: The 'close to the soul' line is about the neck. רבא even went out of his way to get neck meat.

phrases.english: Rava said to his attendant:
When you bring me a piece of meat,
make the effort and bring me one
from the place close to the 'Baruch' spot.
phrases.notes: The neck, where the שוחט says the ברכה over the שחיטה.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows רבא acting on רב אחא בר יעקב's explanation.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In practice, רבא chose neck meat, the part 'close to the soul.'

steps.title: Cabbage for food, beets for healing
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the next line of the list: cabbage is for nourishment and beets are for healing.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'Cabbage is for food, and beets are for healing.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the next line of the list. This sets up the question that comes right after it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Read simply, the line seems to divide the jobs. Cabbage is food and beets are medicine. That split is what the גמרא will challenge in the next step.

phrases.english: Cabbage for food, and beets for healing.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves to the next line in the same list.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Cabbage is described as food and beets as medicine.

steps.title: A ברייתא lists cabbage as a real cure
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: does cabbage only count as food and not as medicine? A ברייתא lists cabbage among the things that truly heal a sick person.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is cabbage for food, yes, but not for healing? But a ברייתא teaches: Six things heal a sick person from his illness, and their healing is a real healing. They are: cabbage, beets, chamomile water, honey, the stomach, the womb, and the lobe of the liver!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the line from step 34. It brings a ברייתא that clearly calls cabbage a cure.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 34 seemed to say cabbage is only food, while beets are the medicine. The ברייתא puts cabbage right next to beets as a true cure. So the simple reading of step 34 cannot be right.

keyTerms.meaning: But a ברייתא teaches (introduces a contradicting source)
Their healing is a real healing
Chamomile water (a kind of herb water)

phrases.english: Cabbage for food, yes,
but for healing, no?
But it was taught in a baraita:

phrases.aramaic: שִׁשָּׁה דְּבָרִים מְרַפְּאִין אֶת הַחוֹלֶה מֵחׇלְיוֹ
phrases.english: Six things heal a sick person from his illness
and their healing is a real healing,
and these are they:
cabbage and beets
and chamomile water, honey,
phrases.notes: How the items are counted to reach 'six' is discussed by the commentators.

phrases.english: and the stomach, and the womb,
and the lobe of the liver!

steps.triggerLanguage: כְּרוּב לְמָזוֹן אִין, וְלִרְפוּאָה לָא? וְהָא תַּנְיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the plain reading of the line in step 34.
steps.kashyaTarget: The reading that cabbage is only for food and not for healing.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A ברייתא counts cabbage among the six things that truly heal, so cabbage must be medicine too.

steps.title: Read it as 'cabbage is even for food'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rereads the line: cabbage is good even as food, and of course it is also medicine.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, say: 'Cabbage is even for food.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by changing how we read the line from step 34.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now the line does not say cabbage is only food. It says cabbage heals, and it is even good as plain food. Beets heal too, but they do not also give nourishment, so the line now fits with the ברייתא.
steps.whatToRemember: Cabbage is both medicine and food. Beets are medicine only. 'Cabbage for food' really means 'cabbage is even for food.'

phrases.english: Rather, say:
'Cabbage is even for food.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge from step 35.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The line meant that cabbage is only food and not medicine.
steps.terutzMaskana: Cabbage is medicine and even food. Beets are medicine only.

steps.title: Woe to the house where turnip passes through
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the next line of the food list: turnip in a house is a bad thing.
steps.simpleTranslation: Woe to the house through which the turnip passes.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא keeps going through its list of foods and quotes a line that warns against turnip (לפת). This sets up the question that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Up to now the list has described foods that heal or nourish. This line says the opposite about turnip: according to רש״י the 'house' is the belly of the person who eats it, so turnip passing through it is harmful.

keyTerms.meaning: Passes through it, meaning it is eaten there regularly

phrases.english: Woe to the house
through which the turnip passes,
phrases.notes: רש״י: the 'house' is the belly of the one who eats turnip.

steps.triggerLanguage: אוֹי לוֹ לַבַּיִת שֶׁהַלֶּפֶת עוֹבֶרֶת בְּתוֹכוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues quoting the food list after the line about cabbage and beets.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Turnip is harmful to the stomach of the one who eats it.

steps.title: But רבא told his servant to always buy turnip
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the line: רבא told his servant that whenever turnip is in the market, buy it for his bread.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is that so? But רבא said to his servant: When you see turnip in the market, don't ask me 'what should I wrap your bread with?' (Just buy the turnip.)
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks how turnip can be harmful if רבא treated it as his favorite food to eat with bread.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא told his servant not to even ask what to serve with his bread when turnip was available; turnip was the automatic choice. A great חכם would not eat something harmful, so this seems to contradict the warning against turnip.

phrases.english: Is that so?!
But Rava said to his servant:
When you see turnip in the market,
do not ask me, 'With what will you wrap your bread?'
phrases.notes: Meaning: don't ask what to serve, just buy the turnip.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִינִי?! וְהָא אָמַר לֵיהּ רָבָא לְשַׁמָּעֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the warning against turnip.
steps.kashyaTarget: The statement that turnip is harmful to a house.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבא's behavior shows turnip is a good, desirable food, which contradicts calling it harmful.

steps.title: Turnip is harmful only without meat or without wine
steps.stepSummary: אביי says turnip is harmful only when eaten without meat; רבא says only without wine.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: It is harmful when eaten without meat. And רבא said: Without wine.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that turnip is not harmful by itself. It is only harmful when eaten without something that protects against it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: According to אביי, meat cancels the harm; according to רבא, wine does. רבא ate turnip with the right food alongside it, so there is no contradiction.

phrases.english: Abaye said: Without meat.
And Rava said: Without wine.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge from רבא's servant.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the case: the harm applies only when turnip is eaten without a protecting food.
steps.terutzMaskana: Turnip is harmful only without meat (אביי) or without wine (רבא).

steps.title: רב, שמואל, and רבי יוחנן on what makes turnip harmful
steps.stepSummary: A parallel dispute is quoted: רב says without meat, שמואל says without wood (not cooked enough), רבי יוחנן says without wine.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was stated: רב said: Without meat. שמואל said: Without wood. And רבי יוחנן said: Without wine.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings the same question from earlier אמוראים, who give three opinions on what turnip needs so it won't harm.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב matches אביי (meat) and רבי יוחנן matches רבא (wine). שמואל adds a new idea: 'without wood' means the turnip was not cooked long enough, so lots of firewood is what fixes it.

keyTerms.meaning: Without wood, meaning not cooked enough

phrases.english: It was stated: Rav said: Without meat.
And Shmuel said: Without wood.
phrases.notes: Meaning it was not cooked thoroughly.

phrases.english: And Rabbi Yochanan said: Without wine.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings an earlier, parallel version of the same answer with a third opinion added.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Turnip's harm is removed by meat (רב), thorough cooking (שמואל), or wine (רבי יוחנן).

steps.title: רבא asks רב פפא how he breaks the turnip's harm
steps.stepSummary: רבא says he uses meat and wine to break the turnip's harm, and asks רב פפא, who doesn't have much wine, what he uses.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said to רב פפא: Brewer! We break the turnip's harm with meat and wine. You, who don't have much wine, what do you break it with?
steps.whatsHappening: רבא opens a short conversation with רב פפא to find out how someone without wine protects himself from turnip. This sets up רב פפא's answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא follows both opinions, meat and wine. רב פפא brewed beer, not wine, so רבא asks what he relies on instead.

keyTerms.meaning: Brewer (a nickname; רב פפא made beer)

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רָבָא לְרַב פָּפָּא: סוּדָנִי,
phrases.english: Rava said to Rav Pappa: Brewer,
we break its harm with meat and wine;
you, who do not have much wine,
with what do you break it?

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רָבָא לְרַב פָּפָּא: סוּדָנִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies the opinions about turnip to real life.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: How someone without wine neutralizes the turnip's harm.

steps.title: רב פפא: we break it with lots of wood
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא answers that he uses wood, meaning long cooking; his wife cooked turnip with eighty Persian logs.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: With wood. Like רב פפא's wife: after she cooked the turnip, she would break its harm by cooking it with eighty Persian logs.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא answers that he follows שמואל's way: cooking the turnip very thoroughly with a lot of firewood.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This shows שמואל's opinion in practice. Without wine, the turnip's harm is removed by heavy cooking, and רב פפא's wife used a huge amount of wood to make sure.

phrases.english: He said to him: With wood,
like this: Rav Pappa's wife,
after she cooked it,
would break it with eighty Persian logs.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רבא's question.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: With wood: very thorough cooking, as שמואל said.
steps.whatToRemember: Turnip is only harmful when eaten without meat, without wine, or undercooked. רבא used meat and wine; רב פפא used very long cooking.

steps.title: A small salted fish can kill on certain days
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that a small salted fish can be deadly on the 7th, 17th, and 27th day after salting; some say the 23rd.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן taught: A small salted fish sometimes kills, on the seventh, seventeenth, and twenty-seventh day. Some say: the twenty-third.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a new food topic and quotes a ברייתא warning that small salted fish can be dangerous on certain days after it was salted.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is a new health warning, not connected to the turnip. The danger depends on how many days have passed since the fish was salted, and there are two versions of the exact days.

phrases.english: The Sages taught: A small salted fish
sometimes kills
on the seventh, the seventeenth, and the twenty-seventh day.
phrases.notes: Counted from when it was salted.

phrases.english: And some say: on the twenty-third.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new food-related topic.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A small salted fish can be deadly on specific days after salting.

steps.title: The danger applies only if the fish was not roasted well
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא limits the danger: it applies only to fish that is half-roasted, not to fish roasted well.
steps.simpleTranslation: We only said this when it was roasted but not properly roasted. But if it was roasted well, we have no concern.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא narrows the warning so it only covers fish that was not cooked properly.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Fish that was roasted thoroughly is safe on any day. The danger is only for fish that was partly roasted.

keyTerms.meaning: We only said this when (limits a rule)
We have no concern with it

phrases.aramaic: וְלָא אֲמַרַן אֶלָּא בְּמִטְּוֵי וְלָא מִטְּוֵי,
phrases.english: And we only said this when it is roasted yet not roasted,
phrases.notes: Meaning half-roasted, not properly cooked.

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל מִטְּוֵי שַׁפִּיר — לֵית לַן בַּהּ.
phrases.english: but if it is roasted well, we have no concern.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְלָא אֲמַרַן אֶלָּא בְּמִטְּוֵי וְלָא מִטְּוֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Limits the danger stated in the ברייתא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Only fish that was not roasted well is dangerous.

steps.title: Even poorly roasted fish is safe if followed by beer
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא adds: even poorly roasted fish is dangerous only if no beer was drunk after it.
steps.simpleTranslation: And for fish not roasted well, we only said this when one did not drink beer after it. But if one drank beer after it, we have no concern.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds a second limit: drinking beer after the fish removes the danger.
steps.deeperAnalysis: So the danger exists only when both things happen: the fish was poorly roasted and no beer was drunk afterward. Either good roasting or beer makes it safe, much like meat, wine, or wood protected against turnip.

phrases.english: And when it is not roasted well,

phrases.aramaic: לָא אֲמַרַן אֶלָּא דְּלָא שְׁתָה בָּתְרֵיהּ שִׁכְרָא,
phrases.english: we only said this when one did not drink beer after it,

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל שְׁתָה בָּתְרֵיהּ שִׁכְרָא — לֵית לַן בַּהּ.
phrases.english: but if one drank beer after it, we have no concern.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּדְלָא מִטְּוֵי שַׁפִּיר, לָא אֲמַרַן אֶלָּא דְּלָא שְׁתָה בָּתְרֵיהּ שִׁכְרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a second limit to the fish danger.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Poorly roasted small salted fish is dangerous only if no beer is drunk afterward.
steps.whatToRemember: The small salted fish is dangerous only when it is both poorly roasted and not followed by beer.

steps.title: What does 'for his thirst' come to exclude?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה about someone who drinks water לצמאו and asks what case the extra word 'for his thirst' is meant to leave out.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: 'One who drinks water for his thirst, etc.' What does this come to exclude?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to a line in the משנה and asks a question about one detail in its wording. This question sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה could have just said 'one who drinks water.' Instead it added 'לצמאו', for his thirst. The גמרא assumes an extra word teaches something, so it asks which kind of water-drinking is left out of the ברכה rule.

keyTerms.meaning: For his thirst; to quench his thirst
Etc.; the quote from the משנה continues
What does it come to exclude?

steps.confusionAlert: The question is not whether drinking water needs a ברכה. The משנה already said it does. The only question is what the word 'for his thirst' leaves out.

phrases.english: [The משנה said:] 'And one who drinks water for his thirst, etc.'
phrases.notes: A quote from the משנה. In full: he says שהכל נהיה בדברו; רבי טרפון says בורא נפשות רבות.

phrases.english: What does this come to exclude?
phrases.notes: The גמרא focuses on the extra word 'for his thirst'.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the topic of turnips and salted fish and returns to explaining the משנה.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which case of drinking water is left out by the משנה's word 'לצמאו'.

steps.title: רב אידי בר אבין begins: it excludes a certain person
steps.stepSummary: רב אידי בר אבין starts to answer: the word 'for his thirst' excludes a certain person. The description of that person continues on the next amud.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אידי בר אבין said: It comes to exclude one who...
steps.whatsHappening: רב אידי בר אבין begins to answer the question from the last step. His sentence is cut off here and finishes on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The answer will name a person who drinks water for some reason other than thirst. Because that person is not drinking for enjoyment, he would not need a ברכה. The rest of the sentence, which tells us who this person is, comes next.

keyTerms.meaning: To exclude one who... (the sentence continues)

steps.confusionAlert: The sentence is not finished. Do not try to work out the answer yet. The case of the excluded person comes on the next amud.

phrases.english: Rav Idi bar Avin said:
It comes to exclude one [who...]
phrases.notes: The sentence continues on the next amud.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר רַב אִידֵּי בַּר אָבִין לְאַפּוֹקֵי לְמַאן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Directly answers the question of what 'לצמאו' excludes.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The word excludes a certain person who does not drink to quench thirst. That person is described on the next amud.
